title: Canon Synthesis Checkpoints
intro: These paired-source checkpoints ask the learner to carry a reading habit across genres. They are not personal legal guidance.

checkpoints.title: A verse becomes a practice

sources.hebrew: שמע ישראל ה׳ אלהינו ה׳ אחד
sources.translation: Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
From when do we recite Shema in the evening?

checkpoints.prompt: What is the most accurate connection between these sources?
choices: The Mishnah treats the Torah verse as a lived practice and asks about its time boundary.
The Mishnah replaces the Torah verse.
The two sources have no meaningful relationship.
checkpoints.explanation: Integrated learning keeps the distinct genre of each source visible while tracing reception.

checkpoints.title: Command and liturgical response

sources.translation: You shall eat, be satisfied, and bless.

checkpoints.prompt: Which reading move best joins the sources?
choices: Trace how a command to bless is later encountered through a form of direct liturgical praise.
Assume the formula makes the verse irrelevant.
Treat both as a Talmudic objection.
checkpoints.explanation: A source chain lets the learner distinguish command, later formulation, and lived practice.

checkpoints.title: Ethics and legal language

sources.translation: With justice shall you judge your fellow.

sources.hebrew: והוי דן את כל האדם לכף זכות

checkpoints.prompt: What makes this a responsible comparison?
choices: Ask how each source frames judgment, while preserving their distinct settings and purposes.
Say they mean exactly the same thing without reading closely.
Turn either source into immediate personal legal advice.
checkpoints.explanation: Comparison starts with a shared question and then identifies difference in voice, context, and claim.

checkpoints.title: Text, history, and civic life

sources.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.

choices: Who receives the address in exile, and how does that setting shape the command?
Which current policy does the verse automatically settle?
Why history should be ignored.
checkpoints.explanation: Historical context supplies evidence; it does not erase a text's continuing importance.

checkpoints.title: Knowledge, heart, and practice

sources.translation: Know today and bring it back to your heart.

checkpoints.prompt: Which synthesis preserves the sources' seriousness?
choices: Both invite inward formation, but each does so through a distinct claim and practice.
Joy makes knowledge unnecessary.
They are just decorative sayings.
checkpoints.explanation: Synthesis is not flattening: identify a real connection and retain the distinct work of each source.

checkpoints.title: A Torah line inside Gemara

sources.translation: When you lie down and when you rise.

sources.hebrew: דיקא נמי דקתני בשעה שבני אדם נכנסין לאכול פתן בערבי שבתות
sources.translation: It is also precise, for it teaches: when people enter to eat their bread on Shabbat evenings.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the key Gemara reading question here?
choices: What argumentative work does the Torah language do in the discussion of time?
Why translate only one word?
Whether the source is decorative.
checkpoints.explanation: When a verse enters a sugya, identify its role in the active argument before drawing conclusions.

checkpoints.title: One word, multiple frameworks
checkpoints.prompt: A reader calls Abraham's departure 'freedom.' What is the disciplined next move?
choices: Define freedom and show how the verse's language supports or complicates that claim.
Assume the label explains itself.
Stop reading the verse once a theme is named.
checkpoints.explanation: Conceptual vocabulary is useful when it makes a source more legible, not when it replaces close reading.

checkpoints.title: A case becomes a category

sources.hebrew: וְכִי יִגַּח שׁוֹר אֶת אִישׁ אוֹ אֶת אִשָּׁה וָמֵת
sources.translation: When an ox gores a man or a woman and they die.
The ox is not like the maveh.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the key reading move connecting these two sources?
choices: The Torah gives a single case; the Mishnah later organizes it alongside others into a differentiated legal category.
The Mishnah replaces the Torah's case with an unrelated one.
The verse and the Mishnah describe the same ruling in identical language.
checkpoints.explanation: Seeing a single Torah case become part of an organized Mishnaic category is the same move as tracing Shema from verse to Mishnah — the case comes first; the category is the Mishnah's own achievement.

checkpoints.title: The integrated reader
checkpoints.prompt: What does independent Jewish learning mean in Seder?
choices: Reading carefully, retrieving skills, tracing connections, and knowing when to seek guidance or community.
Never consulting another reader.
Having an answer before studying.
checkpoints.explanation: Independence is responsible navigation—not isolation or false certainty.
